analysis.one_liner: Limits tax-exempt social welfare groups to 10% political spending and requires disclosure of large donors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, then died there with no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor from either party.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip the tax exemption from 501(c)(4) "social welfare" nonprofits that spend more than 10% of their money on political activity, and would force any such group that engages in politics to publicly disclose every donor who gave $5,000 or more. It would also write a broad, enforceable definition of "political intervention" into the tax code so that groups cannot hide candidate-focused issue ads as charity work. The aim is to unmask "dark money" — political spending by organizations that currently do not have to say who is paying for it.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters gain the most: they would be able to see, in public tax filings, which wealthy donors and companies are behind the political ads and campaigns now run through tax-exempt nonprofits. Nonprofits that genuinely stick to social welfare work (10% or less political spending) keep their exemption and face no disclosure. Candidates and parties also benefit indirectly, because attack ads funded by hidden money would become traceable.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters who want to see who funds political ads

how_it_helps.text: Any 501(c)(4) nonprofit that spends more than 10% of its total expenditures on political activity loses its tax exemption, capping how much anonymous money can flow through these groups into elections.
501(c)(4) groups that engage in political activity must publicly disclose the name and address of every contributor giving $5,000 or more, ending the anonymity that currently shields large donors.

The bill writes a detailed definition of 'political intervention' into the tax code — covering express advocacy, candidate-focused issue ads that reflect a view on a candidate, and political use of an organization's resources — so groups cannot rebrand electioneering as issue education.
It includes an anti-avoidance rule letting Treasury write regulations to catch groups that try to escape the limits by transferring assets to entities controlled by the same people.

analysis.who_pays: 501(c)(4) political networks and their large donors: groups spending heavily on politics would risk losing tax-exempt status and would have to name donors of $5,000 or more in public filings. Nonprofits in general would bear compliance costs of tracking and reporting political spending under the new definitions, and the IRS would take on new enforcement work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dark money nonprofits and their large donors

drawbacks.text: The new 'political intervention' definition is broad — it captures any paid communication that refers to a candidate and reflects a view — so nonprofit advocacy groups worried that ordinary issue ads and even get-out-the-vote-style work could be swept in, chilling speech until Treasury regulations clarify the line.

Public disclosure of donors giving $5,000 or more extends to small nonprofits that do only modest political work; disclosure regimes of this kind raise privacy and harassment concerns for contributors to controversial causes on all sides.
The bill relies on the IRS to define and police political activity, a task that has repeatedly drawn criticism and litigation whenever the tax agency is asked to judge what counts as politics.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: voters get to see who is bankrolling politically active nonprofits, and heavy political spenders lose a tax break they were never clearly meant to have. The cost falls on politically active nonprofits and their donors, plus compliance and enforcement burdens, and the bill's broad definitions would have needed careful Treasury regulations to avoid sweeping in legitimate nonprofit advocacy. Those design risks are real but secondary to the bill's main purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended, so it died without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Jared Golden of Maine introduced the Crack Down on Dark Money Act on April 30, 2024.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day, which is the standard first step; the committee held no hearing or markup and the bill never reached the House floor.
No other member of the House — Democrat or Republican — signed on as a cosponsor.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and all bills not passed by then expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organizations that spend politically through 501(c)(4) nonprofits, and the donors behind them, are better off: they keep both their tax treatment and their anonymity, and no disclosure requirement was ever enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Politically active nonprofits and their anonymous donors

for.name: Jared Golden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only supporter in Congress; no colleague cosponsored it.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, the bill's only referral destination, never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape is unknowable — the only recorded positions are Golden's sponsorship and zero cosponsors.

industries.industry: Politically active 501(c)(4) nonprofit networks ("dark money" groups)
industries.note: These groups exist in large part to run political campaigns without naming funders; the bill would cap their political spending at 10% of expenditures on pain of losing tax exemption and would unmask donors of $5,000 or more. Their business model depends on the anonymity the bill removes.

industries.industry: Wealthy donors and corporations that fund politics through nonprofits
industries.note: Anyone now routing $5,000-plus contributions through a 501(c)(4) to influence elections without a paper trail would have to be named in public filings, pushing this money toward disclosed channels like PACs and super PACs.

Firms producing candidate-focused ads for nonprofit clients would face new definitional and compliance questions, but the money would not disappear — much of it would shift to channels that still buy their services.
